title: Why should they believe you?
principle: Let buyers check your promise for themselves.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a man named Elisha Otis. In the 1850s, people in America were scared of lifts, because if the rope broke, the lift fell. Otis had built a lift with a safety brake. But after a few early orders, nobody else bought one.

screens.title: The show
screens.text: So in 1854, at a big fair in New York, Otis stood on an open lift platform, high above a crowd. Then he had the rope cut. The platform dropped a little and stopped, because his brake had caught it. He had bet his own life on his claim.

screens.prompt: Otis had a safe lift, but few people were buying it. Why do you think the show worked?

options.label: A big fair gave him a big crowd
Nobody would risk his life on a lie

screens.why: The crowd helped, but here's the real reason. A liar would not risk his life like that. If Otis's claim had been false, he could have died, so people believed him.

screens.title: Costly signals
screens.text: Anyone can say "best quality". It costs nothing to say, so buyers don't believe it. Buyers trust proof that would cost a liar much more than an honest seller. This is called a costly signal. Otis could not have faked standing on that platform.

screens.title: Let them check
screens.text: A small shop doesn't need to put anyone in danger. One easy costly signal is letting buyers check your claim. A milk seller tests the milk with a lactometer in front of you, and a liar would not want that. Buyers see the proof themselves.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Otis sold lifts, but your bakery has the same problem. It's the first week of September. Many vegetarian families in the new colony want eggless cakes. Your cakes really are eggless and cost ₹850. But families ask, "How do we know?"

screens.prompt: Families ask how they can know your ₹850 cake is really eggless. Which answer will they believe most?

options.label: Write "100% eggless, I promise" in big letters on every post
Ask five regular buyers to share reviews of the taste
Let families watch their cake being made on live video

screens.why: Yes. On a live video, families watch their own cake being made and see every ingredient go in. They can see for themselves instead of trusting your words.

wrong.a: Anyone can write "I promise". It costs nothing, so a careful family won't believe it. A live video lets them see for themselves.
wrong.b: Reviews help, and you'll learn more about them soon. But a review can't prove there's no egg in this family's cake. A live video of their own cake lets them check.

screens.prompt: Your sister says, "Spend ₹8,000 on a 'pure eggless' ad." Your friend says, "Pay ₹5,000 if a food lab finds egg." Who's right?

options.label: Your sister: pay for the big ad

screens.why: Right. Any family can send a slice to a lab. If you're honest, you won't have to pay the ₹5,000, but a liar could lose a lot. An ad costs an honest shop and a liar the same, so it proves nothing.

wrong.a: The ad costs money, but it costs an honest shop and a liar the same, so it proves nothing. Your friend's promise would only cost a liar, so families believe it.
wrong.c: Words alone may not work, but this promise is different. A liar would lose ₹5,000 each time a lab finds egg, so families believe it.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things a baker might do. For each one, tell me: can buyers check it, or must they trust you?

items.text: A live video of the cake being baked
"Made with love" printed on the box
List every ingredient and show the packs
Taste a slice of the same cake before paying

screens.why: Buyers can check a video, the packs you show and a taste before paying. But anyone can say "made with love", "freshest" or "always happy". Buyers can't check these words, so they must trust you.

screens.setup: A week later, a chain bakery opens near the colony. Its cakes cost ₹700, and its sign says "pure butter". Your cakes use real butter. They cost ₹400 to make and sell for ₹850. You sell 20 a week. A mother says, "They say butter too, and they're cheaper."
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Cut your cake to ₹700 to match them
options.outcome: You still sell 20 cakes a week, but each now leaves you ₹300, not ₹450. That's ₹6,000 a week, not ₹9,000. Families still can't tell which bakery uses real butter.
options.why: Cutting the price didn't prove anything. You lost ₹3,000 a week, and buyers still couldn't see the difference.
options.better: Let families check: show the butter packs and the baking.

options.label: Ask 10 happy buyers to post "real butter" reviews
options.outcome: Families have heard "pure butter" from both of you. 3 of your 20 weekly buyers try the chain. You sell 17 cakes, leaving you ₹7,650 a week.
options.why: You kept your price, but reviews just repeated your words, and the chain has happy buyers too. Nothing showed which claim was true.
options.better: Let families check: show the butter packs and the baking.

options.label: Show the butter packs in every baking video
options.outcome: Families see the butter packs and the bill in every video. A mother asks the chain shop to show the same, and it has no packs or bills to show. You keep all 20 weekly buyers at ₹850, leaving you ₹9,000 a week.
options.why: You showed proof that buyers could check. Now the chain's claim is harder to believe than yours.

screens.text: Words cost ___, so buyers believe proof they can ___ for themselves.
screens.why: Exactly. Otis let the crowd see his brake work. You let families watch their own cake being made and see the butter packs. Proof that buyers can check is a costly signal an honest shop can afford.

summary: Costly signal: proof that would cost a liar a lot. Buyers believe it more than words.
An ad costs an honest shop and a liar the same, so it proves nothing.
Let buyers check your claim themselves. Show a live video of their cake, the packs you use, or a taste before paying.

cards.front: A ghee seller wants buyers to believe it's pure. What works best?
options: Put "100% pure" on a big sign
Show the lab report for this batch
cards.back: Let buyers check the claim themselves. Words cost nothing, so they prove nothing.

cards.front: Which promise is a costly signal?
options: Pay ₹5,000 to anyone who finds a fault
cards.back: A costly signal costs only a liar. An ad costs an honest shop and a liar the same.

cards.front: A rival also says "pure butter". How do you prove your claim?
cards.back: When both make the same claim, buyers believe the one who shows proof.
